final_answer:
Flow of the argumentation

1) Opinions put forward (pro-AI, ag1)
- Main pro-claims:
  - AI improves everyday life by adding convenience.
  - AI improves health and standard of living.
  - AI makes work easier for students and professionals.
  - AI helps marginalized groups, especially by offering accessibility for people with disabilities.
  - AI can improve workplace safety.
  - Additional pro-claims:
    - AI can reduce barriers to education and training.
    - AI can make learning more inclusive via personalized assistance.
    - AI can improve access to services through tools and automation (helping people facing obstacles).
- Final synthesis by ag1:
  - Even if AI has downsides, AI is good for society *if* we mitigate economic harm, privacy risks, and bias while preserving benefits for inclusion and improved access.

2) Objections raised (anti-AI, ag2)
- Main objections:
  - AI harms the economic well-being of many people and businesses.
    - From this, ag2 concludes: AI is not good for society.
  - AI poses dangerous privacy risks.
    - From this, ag2 concludes: AI is harmful to society / harmful to personal privacy.
  - AI undermines critical thinking skills for students and adults.
    - Leads to: AI is harmful to education and public reasoning.
  - AI harms racial minorities by repeating and exacerbating racism.
    - Leads to: AI is harmful to racial equality.
- Anti conclusion:
  - Because these harms supposedly occur together (economic harm, harm to education/reasoning, racial inequality, privacy harm), ag2 concludes: AI is not good for society.

3) How each objection was answered (ag1’s rebuttals)
- ag1 produced a rebuttal that mirrors the pro-case:
  - It reiterates the claimed benefits: convenience, health/standard of living, work/school assistance, disability accessibility, and improved workplace safety.
- ag1 then introduces an important “mitigation” strategy:
  - It concedes the existence of the negative factors mentioned by ag2 (economic harm, privacy risks, bias/racism) in the form of a conditional:
    - AI is good for society *if we mitigate* these harms while preserving benefits.

What remains undecided
- The debate does not establish whether mitigation is realistically achievable at scale, fast enough, and with sufficient reliability.
  - ag2’s case treats the harms as straightforwardly harmful; ag1 does not provide evidence that mitigation will actually occur or will be effective in practice.
- It remains undecided whether the alleged cognitive/educational harm (“undermines critical thinking”) is significant enough to outweigh the educational accessibility/personalization benefits.
- It remains undecided whether AI-driven labor/economic disruption will be accompanied by adequate compensation, retraining, or redistribution to prevent net harm.
- It remains undecided whether privacy risks can be controlled to a level acceptable to society, given real-world incentives and governance challenges.

What is known (from the arguments themselves)
- Known from ag1’s side:
  - There are plausible channels for AI to benefit society: convenience, health/quality-of-life improvements, productivity/assistance for education and work, better accessibility for people with disabilities, and safety improvements.
  - ag1’s stance is conditional: AI is good if harms (economic, privacy, bias) are mitigated.
- Known from ag2’s side:
  - The main risks raised are concrete categories: economic harm, privacy harm, educational/public reasoning harm, and racial bias/exacerbated racism.
  - ag2’s stance is categorical: these harms imply AI is not good for society.

Bottom line
- The argumentation ended without full justification because the pro side relied mainly on asserted benefits and a conditional mitigation principle, while the con side raised harms and asserted they make AI not good—yet no side conclusively proved which side dominates under real-world deployment and governance. The main unresolved question is whether effective mitigation of the harms is realistically achievable.
